ex-swift-if-let: Optional binding runs a block only when the optional has a value.
It's the same keyword you'd use for any condition; Swift 5.7+ lets you write just `___ let name` without `= name`.
ex-swift-guard: This is an early exit: check the condition up front and leave if it fails.
Blank 1 is the keyword for an early-exit check; blank 2 is the word that introduces the block that runs when the check fails.
ex-swift-map: You want a new array with every element transformed.
The higher-order function that transforms each element and returns an array of the results.
ex-swift-mutating: Struct methods can't change stored properties by default.
Mark the method with the keyword that lets a value-type method modify `self`.
ex-python-def: Every Python function starts with a keyword.
ex-python-comprehension: A list comprehension reads like: value, loop, optional filter.
Blank 1 starts the loop over `numbers`; blank 2 starts the filter condition.
ex-python-dict-get: Reading a missing key with `counts[word]` raises `KeyError`.
Use the dict method that returns a default value when the key isn't there.
ex-alg-binary-search: The loop must still run when the range has one item left.
Blank 1 compares `low` and `high` so equal still loops; blank 2 moves past `mid`, since `mid` was already checked.
ex-alg-factorial: Recursion needs a stopping value and a smaller subproblem.
0! and 1! are both the same small number; the recursive call works on the number just below `n`.
ex-ds-stack: A stack adds and removes at the same end: last in, first out.
Array methods: one adds at the end, the other removes the last element and returns it as an optional.
ex-ds-queue: A queue is first in, first out: take from the front.
`deque` has a pop method for the left end.
ex-oop-inheritance: Java has a keyword for "is a subclass of".
It's the keyword for class inheritance, not the one for interfaces.
ex-db-where: SQL filters rows with a clause after `FROM`.
The clause that keeps only rows matching a condition.
ex-db-order-limit: You need to sort the rows, then keep only the first few.
Blank 1 is the two-word sorting clause; blank 2 caps the number of rows returned.
ex-db-placeholder: Never paste user input into SQL; pass it as a parameter instead.
sqlite3 uses a single-character placeholder for each value in the tuple.
ex-db-group-by: `COUNT(*)` per customer means collapsing rows into one group per customer.
The two-word clause that groups rows by a column's value.
ex-net-tcp-socket: TCP is a reliable, connection-based byte stream.
Choose the socket type constant for streams (UDP would be datagrams).
ex-net-http-status: The response object knows the HTTP status code the server sent.
Read it as an attribute named for what it is (200, 404, …).
ex-net-success-range: Every 2xx code is from 200 up to, but not including, 300.
Write a Swift range: half-open `..<` or closed `...`.
ex-os-thread-join: A thread does nothing until it's started, and the main thread doesn't wait unless told to.
Blank 1 begins running `work`; blank 2 blocks until the thread finishes.
ex-os-lock: Only one thread at a time should run `count += 1`.
Use the statement that acquires the lock and releases it automatically at the end of the block.
ex-os-async-let: `async let` starts both tasks; you still have to wait for their results.
The keyword that suspends until async values are ready (alongside `try`).
ex-oop-protocol: A struct adopts a protocol by listing it after a colon.
Write the name of the protocol it should conform to.
ex-oop-override: Java has an annotation that says "this replaces the parent's method".
It starts with `@`, and the compiler checks the parent really has that method.
ex-oop-init: Python calls a special method when an object is created.
The constructor's name has two underscores on each side.
ex-java-for-each: Java's enhanced for loop reads "for each score in scores".
One punctuation character separates the variable from the collection.
ex-java-implements: A class promises to provide an interface's methods.
For interfaces Java uses a different keyword than `extends`.
ex-java-catch: `try` needs a handler for the exception it might throw.
The block that handles a specific exception type after `try`.
ex-java-get-or-default: `counts.get(word)` returns `null` for a new word, and `null + 1` crashes.
Use the `Map` method that returns a fallback value when the key is missing.
ex-cpp-swap-ref: By default C++ passes copies, so changing them doesn't affect the caller.
Make each parameter a reference with the same symbol in both places.
ex-cpp-push-back: You want to add an element to the end of the vector.
The `std::vector` method that appends (or constructs in place) at the back.
ex-cpp-unique-ptr: A smart pointer that owns its object frees it when it goes out of scope.
ex-cpp-const-ref: Bind each element as a reference you can't modify (`const` plus `&`).
ex-git-stage: Git has a staging area between your files and a commit.
The git command that stages changes; `.` means everything.
ex-git-commit: Staged changes are saved into history by one command.
The git command that records a snapshot; `-m` gives its message.
ex-git-branch: `git switch` changes branches; a flag makes it create the branch first.
The short flag is one letter (the long form is `--create`).
ex-sec-param-query: Building SQL with string concatenation allows SQL injection.
Use the driver's placeholder and pass `email` in the tuple.
ex-sec-escape-html: Characters like `<` and `>` in user input can become HTML tags.
The `html` module function that turns them into entities like `<`.
ex-sec-compare-digest: `==` can stop at the first different character, which leaks timing.
ex-sec-hash-password: A salt must be random and unpredictable.
Use the `os` function that returns cryptographically secure random bytes.
ex-ds-linked-list: Each node in a singly linked list points to the following node.
The line below sets `head.next`, so name the property to match.
ex-ds-set: You only care about distinct values, not how many times each appears.
Convert the list to the built-in collection that drops duplicates.
ex-ds-heap: A heap needs its own push function to stay ordered.
The `heapq` function that adds an item; it pairs with `heappop`.
ex-alg-swap: Arrays have a method that exchanges two elements by index.
Its name says "swap" and "at" two positions.
ex-alg-two-sum: You're checking whether the complement was already seen.
Python's membership operator tests whether a key is in a dict.
ex-alg-memo: Memoization stores each result the first time it's computed.
`functools` has a decorator (Python 3.9+) that caches every call's result.
ex-os-semaphore: A lock allows one thread at a time; you want a counter that allows three.
The `threading` class that keeps N permits.
ex-os-env: Use the dict method that takes a default for a missing key.
ex-db-join: The rows you need come from two tables matched on `customer_id`.
The keyword that combines tables using the `ON` condition.
ex-oop-abstract: `Shape` can't compute an area itself; subclasses must.
A class with an abstract method must itself be marked with the same keyword.
ex-net-json-decode: Call its method that takes the type and the data.
ex-net-json-loads: `json` can parse a string or a file.
Use the function for a string: it ends in "s".
ex-swift-switch-result: Each pattern in a Swift `switch` starts with the same keyword.
Write the keyword that begins a branch, as in the `.success` line above it.
ex-python-fstring: Python formats `{name}` in a string only when it's a formatted string literal.
Put a single-letter prefix right before the opening quote.
ex-python-except: `try` needs a handler for the error that `int()` raises.
Python's keyword for catching an exception type.
